intro.title: MemoryWeft Manager
intro.lede: A tool for managing your local MemoryWeft MCP server. New here? Read the guide below, then prepare your DB and project in the Settings tab.
intro.k2g.title: K2G — Knowledge To Graph
intro.k2g.body:
A RAG-based Edge-Centric Knowledge Graph (ECKG) engine developed by OnMinimum. It analyzes documents and conversations as narratives of events in which multiple objects participate.
  • Objects appearing in a document/conversation = entities
  • The document/conversation itself = an event (acting as an edge that binds entities together)
Entities and events together form two kinds of graph.
  • Entity–entity graph — entities linked by event edges. Shows “who was involved with whom, in what event, and how”.
  • Event–event graph — events linked by entity edges. Shows how independent events connect through shared entities.
Both entities and events carry embedding vectors — you can find events with similar context and semantically close entities by vector.
intro.mw.title: MemoryWeft — Memory built for AI
intro.mw.body: An AI-dedicated long-term memory built on the K2G engine. It evolves an AI's memory from prompt / RAG based to graph based. Beyond simple search, it uses organic, connection-based retrieval to weave the context of your work or organization.
intro.mcp.title: Using MCP
intro.mcp.body:
MCP is the standard by which an AI calls external tools. Just speak naturally and the AI picks the right tool; starting with “mw …” makes it clear you mean a memory action.
  1. Search (mw search) — word & sentence search. Not plain search but graph-based results, with related entity and connection hints.
  2. Save / recall (mw save · mw recall) — say “mw save” for an important point in a chat and it is stored as an event. Call “mw recall” and the AI searches related content and folds it into its answer.
  3. Cluster summary (mw cluster / auto-tag summary) — ask “mw summarize the clusters” and it summarizes the Leiden community structure (event & entity clusters, auto-tags) — cluster count, sizes, and representative members. See the whole topic landscape of your memory at a glance.
  4. Document ingestion (“load this document into memory”) — point the AI at a file or document and say “ingest this into memory”; it organizes the content and loads it for you. You can hand it several files at once.
Note · On first run, loading the embedding model can take a while (BGE-M3, 2–5 min). If the connection is slow, try reconnecting.
intro.av.title: Antivirus / security software
intro.av.body:
The first run — or the first connection right after a reboot — can be slow because antivirus software (e.g. Windows Defender) scans the embedding model, runtime libraries, and DB files on first open; once scanned, it is fast.
· If it is slow on every cold boot, add the install folder and data folder to your antivirus's real-time scan exclusions to greatly speed up cold start.
· On macOS, Gatekeeper / quarantine checks can cause a similar one-time first-run delay.
intro.db.title: Database
intro.db.body:
K2G stores information in a database. It currently supports:
  • SQLite — local file based. Plenty for personal use. Single-user only — concurrent multi-user use is prohibited: if several people write to the same DB at once (concurrent ingest) it causes lock conflicts and errors.
  • PostgreSQL — usable in the cloud. For concurrent multi-user access, always use PostgreSQL.
· SQLite placed on a cloud drive is not recommended — concurrent writes can conflict.
· For K2G, network egress/ingress size matters more than DB capacity. Check traffic limits when using an external DB.
intro.pg.title: Postgres — share across machines & teams
intro.pg.body:
• With a cloud Postgres DB, your AI memory follows you even when you switch computers.
  • A team can share one working memory. (Tip: give each member a different personal Tag.)
  • Cloud Postgres has many free or low-cost providers — pick one that fits and decide on your DB. (Tip: if you need help setting up the DB, ask your AI.)
  • A Postgres DSN is as sensitive as a password. Keep it from being exposed.
intro.org.title: Organizing & checking your memory
intro.org.body:
A database (DB) is where memories live. You can organize it by purpose, in three ways:
  • Separate DBs — keep a distinct database per project, organization, or personal use.
  • Split by domain — partition a single DB into domains so they never bleed into each other.
  • Group / Tag — within one DB, separate by topic using Groups or Tags while keeping them interrelated. Assign a topic or author as a Tag.
To review what has been stored, go to Search → Event search and click Search with no filters to list everything.
intro.must.title: Must-knows
intro.must.body:
1. Define your domains.
    A domain is a global separator for partitioning data. Keep content that must not mix (e.g. work vs personal) in separate domains.
  2. Predefine your tags.
    The AI automatically extracts important entities from events. But information that cannot be extracted from the content — such as a project name or author — must be set up as tags in advance. Predefined tags are stored alongside events regardless of their content. The AI may also attach appropriate tags automatically on save.
  3. You can add/remove tags.
    If an AI-generated tag looks wrong, delete it in the Edit tab.
  4. Delete entities with care.
    Deleting an entity severs its event links and changes the graph structure. Delete only what you've explicitly judged unnecessary. For duplicate entities, merge instead of delete. A merge can be partly undone (the name can be restored), but the linked events cannot be restored.

an.title: Analysis
an.lede:
Cluster the entities/events stored in a domain for analysis. Pick suitable parameters and save them.
Exclude entities that disrupt graph formation from the computation.
Background-word entities that attach everywhere clump the graph into one blob, making topic separation hard.
an.params.title: Leiden parameters
an.params.desc: Runs the Leiden algorithm on the event/entity graph to form similar clusters. Higher resolution = finer clusters, lower = coarser. Seed is for reproducibility. Entity similarity threshold connects two events only if their shared-entity similarity (jaccard) is at or above this value — lower values link weaker similarities, yielding more clusters and lower modularity (event graph only). Use 0.4 for entity-dense domains like code/docs, 0.05 for topic-scattered conversation memory.
an.params.thetaEHint: Connect two events only if their shared-entity similarity (jaccard) ≥ this value (0-1). Lower = connect weaker similarities (more communities, lower modularity). Code/docs ≈ 0.4, sparse conversation memory ≈ 0.05.
an.scoped.title: Tag-scoped community explore
an.scoped.ephemeralHint: Results in this tab are not persisted (the canonical communities don't change). For freely exploring with different θ_e / resolution / tag.
an.scoped.desc: Runs leiden on demand within the chosen tag boundary only. Results are not persisted (no effect on the canonical auto-tags) — this is an exploration lens. Only human/system-assigned discovery tags are listed.
an.scoped.descTags: Discovery tags are high-value tags you explicitly pinned. If you have none, add 'Save tags' in settings.
an.scoped.descAsk: Ask the AI [mw summarize the event cluster for '<tag name>'] and it will summarize and report the contents.
an.scoped.tagNone: No discovery tags — assign one first via curated --tag
an.scoped.thetaEHint: Entity edge threshold for this exploration only. Use 0.05 for conversation memory (content-based communities). No effect on the canonical run.

an.exp.entityCountTitle: Number of entities in this event

an.entity.desc: Select an entity to see the events it appears in, grouped by Leiden community. Click a cluster to see its detailed event list.
an.entity.statusHint: Leave the box empty to show the top 50 by influence.
an.event.statusHint: Recomputes only Event Leiden on top of the current Jaccard (~seconds). Jaccard itself is updated under [Excluded entities → Apply].
an.event.title: Event clusters
an.event.desc:
Event clusters formed by Leiden. If you see a giant cluster, it is usually caused by background words on the entity side — excluding them in the [Excluded entities] tab and recomputing cleans it up automatically.
A giant cluster that still remains is one of:
  • (a) a genuinely abstract group of events
  • (b) a normal topic cluster
Ask "mw summarize this event cluster" in MCP to get a topic summary.
an.sw.desc: Excluding background-word entities that attach everywhere from the Leiden computation can yield much more meaningful results.
an.sw.statusHint:
Load candidates with [Search with Leiden], check the boxes, then press [Apply].
※ [Apply] includes Jaccard recomputation and takes 30s–several minutes.
an.sw.candDesc:
Review and check the boxes.
DF = fraction of all records this entity appears in. Areas = number of topic areas this entity intrudes into. High DF and area counts likely mean an everywhere-attaching background word.

onb.title: Welcome to MWeft
onb.intro: Let's set this project up. A project is one memory database (its own store) with its own settings.
onb.project.title: What a project is
onb.project.body: Each project is an isolated memory store — all memories, entities, and search live inside it. Keep separate projects for work, personal notes, a codebase, and so on.
onb.domain.title: Domain — why it matters
onb.domain.body: A domain is a classification inside a project, like a top-level folder for memories (e.g. "work", "research"). Saves and searches default to the current domain, so unrelated memories don't mix.
onb.domain.label: Default domain
onb.group.title: Group
onb.group.body: A group is a higher-level namespace shared across saves — handy when several projects belong to one initiative. Leave it as "default" if unsure.
onb.group.label: Group
onb.tags.title: Default tags
onb.tags.body: Tags label what a memory is about. Default tags are applied automatically to new saves so you don't tag every time. Comma-separated; leave empty to skip.
onb.tags.label: Default tags
onb.data.title: Data folder
onb.data.bodyNew: Choose a local folder for this project. Its database, the raw memory originals, and the logs are stored here.
onb.data.bodyPg: Postgres keeps the graph/vector data remotely, but each memory's raw original and the logs are still local files. Choose a folder for them.
onb.data.bodyReuse: This project's existing data folder is reused for the raw originals and logs — no extra path needed.
onb.data.label: Local data folder
onb.errData: Enter a local data folder for this project.
onb.db.title: Database
onb.db.body: Where the graph and vectors are stored. SQLite keeps everything in a local file; Postgres uses a server (enter its connection string).
